content: # Programming remote key Mitsubishi Colt 2007 1.3: Why Standard OBD Methods Fail Most online tutorials for programming a remote key on a Mitsubishi Colt from this era rely on a specific sequence: connecting pins 1 and 4 in the OBD-II port, turning the ignition to "ON," and pressing the emergency button inside the door six times. This method works flawlessly on many Mitsubishi models with full-size 16-pin connectors. However, when you physically inspect the OBD port on a Colt 2007 1.3, you will find that pin 4 is absent from the connector layout. This physical absence creates an immediate logical contradiction for the standard procedure. The tutorials assume a continuous circuit exists between the ground (pin 4) and power (pin 1) to complete the loop required by the immobilizer ECU to enter programming mode. Without pin 4, forcing the connection or simply following the video instructions results in no response from the vehicle. The car remains in "accessory" or "off" state, ignoring the button presses entirely. ### Understanding the Electrical Constraint To resolve this, we must look at how the OBD-II specification interacts with legacy automotive wiring. The standard ISO 15765-4 protocol often utilized by these cars expects a specific grounding path through pin 4 to trigger the "Learn Mode." When that pin is missing from the physical plug, the ECU cannot detect the voltage drop or ground shift necessary to acknowledge the command. You might consider using an adapter cable that maps standard OBD pins to the available ones in your specific port. While this works for diagnostics and data reading on modern cars, it rarely solves ignition-based programming sequences. These sequences often rely on shorting specific internal grounds within the ECU chassis. If the car's wiring harness was designed with a 7-pin or 9-pin configuration that omits pin 4, adding an external ground via adapter won't replicate the exact electrical signature the immobilizer module expects to see when it validates the key request. ### Alternative Entry Points and Diagnostics If the standard OBD method is physically impossible due to the missing pin, you need to identify alternative triggers for the immobilizer system. On many Mitsubishi platforms from this generation, the programming mode can be initiated via the ignition switch itself or a specific sequence involving the central locking buttons rather than the emergency flasher button inside the cabin. Check your owner's manual for sequences that do not depend on the OBD port at all. Some models require: 1. Inserting the key and turning to position 1 (ON). 2. Pressing the central locking unlock button a specific number of times (e.g., 6 or 8) while in the ON position. 3. Waiting for the hazard lights to flash three times, indicating readiness. If your model uses an external trunk release switch or a dedicated service port near the battery, these locations often house the same immobilizer logic but with different access points. The goal is to find a method that triggers the ECU's internal flag without relying on the missing OBD pin 4 ground path. ### When to Seek Professional Assistance If you have exhausted documentation and cannot locate an alternative trigger sequence, the issue may stem from a variant of the immobilizer module or a custom wiring modification by a previous owner. In these cases, attempting to force a connection could damage the ECU's communication lines. Professional locksmiths often use specialized diagnostic tools that bypass the OBD port entirely, sending raw signals directly to the immobilizer bus or utilizing proprietary key-on-the-fly protocols. If your Colt requires this level of intervention, it is safer to consult a specialist who has access to the specific wiring diagrams for your 1.3 engine variant.
